subject: Surgery
topic: Cauda Equina Syndrome vs Conus Medullaris Surgical Decompression
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) from Conus Medullaris Syndrome: 1. CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME: compression of lumbosacral nerve roots (L2-S5) BELOW the conus medullaris (below L1-L2 vertebra, e.g., massive central L4-L5 disc herniation, tumor, trauma). Pure LOWER MOTOR NEURON (LMN) lesion: ASYMMETRIC, severe radicular shooting leg pain; asymmetric flaccid leg weakness; HYPOREFLEXIA/AREFLEXIA (absent ankle and knee jerks); SADDLE ANESTHESIA (loss of sensation in S3-S5 dermatomes: perineum, perianal, buttocks, inner thighs); and LATE autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention with overflow incontinence [post-void residual > 200 mL], decreased anal sphincter tone). 2. CONUS MEDULLARIS SYNDROME: injury to distal spinal cord at L1-L2; mixed UMN/LMN, symmetric pain, early fecal/urinary incontinence, bilateral hyperreflexia or Babinski. MANAGEMENT OF CAUDA EQUINA: 1. IMMEDIATE EMERGENT LUMBAR SPINE MRI; 2. EMERGENT SURGICAL DECOMPRESSION (laminectomy/discectomy) WITHIN 24-48 HOURS to prevent permanent paralysis and irreversible bowel/bladder incontinence.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Gouty Arthritis Flare Medical Management Contraindications
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Gout Flare: First-line pharmacotherapy options: 1. NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen); 2. Colchicine; 3. Corticosteroids. SELECTION AND CONTRAINDICATIONS: In a patient with ADVANCED CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (CKD stage 4-5, eGFR < 30 mL/min), heart failure, or active peptic ulcer disease: BOTH NSAIDs (cause acute renal failure via afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction) and COLCHICINE (causes severe neuromyelopathy and fatal bone marrow toxicity due to renal clearance failure) ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED. THE FIRST-LINE TREATMENT OF CHOICE IS SYSTEMIC OR INTRA-ARTICULAR CORTICOSTEROIDS (oral prednisone, intra-articular triamcinolone if 1-2 joints involved). CRUCIAL MANAGEMENT RULE: DO NOT START, STOP, OR ALTER THE DOSE OF URIC ACID-LOWERING DRUGS (ALLOPURINOL, FEBUXOSTAT) DURING AN ACUTE GOUT FLARE! Rapid changes in serum urate destabilize microtophi and prolong/worsen the acute flare.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Hyperkalemia with Electrocardiographic Changes Treatment Sequence
shortestValidSolution: Manage Severe Hyperkalemia: Serum potassium > 6.5 mEq/L, or any potassium level with ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC (ECG) MANIFESTATIONS: peaked T waves -> PR prolongation -> loss of P wave -> QRS widening -> "sine wave" pattern -> ventricular fibrillation / asystole. TREATMENT SEQUENCE: 1. FIRST AND MOST CRITICAL IMMEDIATE STEP: INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM GLUCONATE (or calcium chloride via central line). Calcium STABILIZES THE CARDIOMYOCYTE MEMBRANE within 1 to 3 minutes by raising the threshold potential, preventing fatal ventricular arrhythmias (does NOT lower potassium!); 2. CELLULAR SHIFTING (transcellular drive): Regular insulin (10 units IV) PLUS 50% Dextrose (D50W) (shifts K+ intracellularly via Na+/K+-ATPase within 15-30 minutes); nebulized albuterol; IV sodium bicarbonate (if metabolic acidosis); 3. TOTAL BODY ELIMINATION: Cation-exchange resins (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate / Lokelma), loop diuretics (furosemide), or EMERGENT HEMODIALYSIS (definitive clearance).

subject: Medicine
topic: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis Albumin Infusion and Antibiotic Selection
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP): primary infection of ascitic fluid in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Pathophysiology: bacterial translocation across edematous bowel wall into ascitic fluid. Clinical signs: fever, abdominal pain/tenderness, altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy), or worsening renal function. DIAGNOSTIC GOLD STANDARD: PARACENTESIS demonstrating ASCITIC FLUID ABSOLUTE NEUTROPHIL (PMN) COUNT >= 250/microL (calculated as total WBC * % neutrophils). Bacterial culture most commonly grows E. coli or Klebsiella. MANAGEMENT BUNDLE: 1. Immediate empiric antibiotic therapy: IV 3RD-GENERATION CEPHALOSPORIN (CEFOTAXIME or CEFTRIAXONE); 2. INTRAVENOUS ALBUMIN INFUSION: 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis, followed by 1.0 g/kg on day 3. Albumin expands effective arterial volume, preserves renal perfusion, and PREVENTS HEPATORENAL SYNDROME, significantly reducing mortality from 30% down to 10%!

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Variceal Bleeding Octreotide and Antibiotic Prophylaxis Bundle
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Variceal Upper Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage in cirrhosis: Medical emergency. MANAGEMENT BUNDLE: 1. HEMODYNAMIC RESUSCITATION: Large-bore IV access; RESTRICTIVE RED BLOOD CELL TRANSFUSION (target hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL; liberal transfusion increases portal pressures and triggers rebleeding!); 2. PHARMACOTHERAPY: INTRAVENOUS OCTREOTIDE (somatostatin analog: selectively constricts splanchnic circulation, reducing portal venous inflow and variceal pressure); 3. PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS: INTRAVENOUS CEFTRIAXONE (1 g daily for 7 days) MUST BE ADMINISTERED TO ALL CIRRHOTICS WITH GI BLEEDING (prevents SBP, bacteremia, re-bleeding, and mortality!); 4. DEFINITIVE THERAPY: URGENT UPPER ENDOSCOPY (EGD) within 12 hours with ENDOSCOPIC VARICEAL LIGATION (banding). If refractory bleeding: Balloon tamponade (Blakemore tube) as bridge to emergent TIPS.

topic: Adult Acute Epiglottitis Airway Security Prioritization
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Adult Acute Epiglottitis: life-threatening supraglottic airway infection (caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Staphylococcus aureus). Classic clinical triad: 1. Severe, excruciating SORE THROAT AND ODYNOPHAGIA completely DISPROPORTIONATE TO OROPHARYNGEAL FINDINGS (pharynx looks completely normal on direct inspection!); 2. Inability to swallow secretions, presenting with POOLING OF SALIVA and DROOLING; 3. Respiratory distress with "TRIPOD" POSITIONING (sitting upright, leaning forward, neck extended). Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph demonstrates the "THUMBPRINT SIGN" (swollen, enlarged epiglottis). DECISIVE MANAGEMENT RULE: AIRWAY SECURITY IS THE IMMEDIATE TOP PRIORITY. DO NOT EXAMINE THE PHARYNX WITH A TONGUE BLADE (can precipitate sudden complete laryngospasm and fatal asphyxiation!). Prepare for IMMEDIATELY CONTROLLED ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION OR CRICOTHYROTOMY IN THE OPERATING ROOM with an anesthesiologist and otolaryngologist present.

subject: Medicine
topic: Hypertensive Emergency Blood Pressure Targets Aortic Dissection vs Stroke
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Blood Pressure Management Targets in Hypertensive Emergencies: 1. ACUTE AORTIC DISSECTION: The ONLY hypertensive emergency requiring RAPID, AGGRESSIVE BLOOD PRESSURE LOWERING. Target: SYSTOLIC BLOOD PRESSURE < 120 mm Hg (or 100-110) AND HEART RATE < 60/min WITHIN 20 MINUTES. Utilize IV BETA-BLOCKERS (Esmolol, Labetalol) FIRST to decrease aortic shear stress (dP/dt); add vasodilator (nitroprusside) ONLY AFTER beta-blockade (vasodilators alone cause reflex tachycardia, increasing tear propagation!). 2. ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKE: PERMISSIVE HYPERTENSION is maintained to preserve collateral perfusion in the ischemic penumbra. Do NOT lower blood pressure UNLESS: a) Patient receives IV thrombolytic (tPA / alteplase): BP must be lowered to < 185/110 mm Hg before tPA and kept < 180/105; b) Patient does NOT receive tPA: BP is permitted up to 220/120 mm Hg (lower by only 15% in first 24 hours if > 220/120). 3. General Hypertensive Emergency (encephalopathy, ACS): lower MAP by no more than 20-25% over the first hour.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis Cerebral Edema Complication
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Cerebral Edema in Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): most lethal complication of pediatric DKA (responsible for 60-90% of DKA deaths in children). Risk factors: 1. OVERLY RAPID FLUID ADMINISTRATION (> 4 L/m2/day or rapid infusion of hypotonic fluids); 2. RAPID DROP IN EFFECTIVE SERUM OSMOLALITY; 3. ADMINISTRATION OF INTRAVENOUS SODIUM BICARBONATE (causes paradoxical central nervous system acidosis and rapid cellular swelling); 4. High initial BUN and severe acidemia. CLINICAL SIGNS (typically develop 4-12 hours after starting therapy): sudden onset of severe headache, progressive lethargy/irritability, bradycardia and hypertension (Cushing reflex), decreased consciousness, incontinence, and pupillary asymmetry/sluggishness. IMMEDIATE TREATMENT: 1. STOP OR SLOW IV FLUIDS; 2. IMMEDIATE INTRAVENOUS MANNITOL (0.5-1.0 g/kg over 20 minutes) or 3% HYPERTONIC SALINE (3-5 mL/kg). DO NOT WAIT FOR CT SCAN TO INITIATE OSMOTHERAPY!

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Ingested Foreign Body Button Battery vs Coin Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Ingested Button Battery from Coin in the Esophagus: 1. ESOPHAGEAL BUTTON BATTERY: TRUE SURGICAL EMERGENCY! Mechanism of rapid injury: generates an external electrical circuit when touching mucosal tissue, hydrolyzing tissue water and generating HYDROXIDE (OH-) IONS at the negative pole (anode) -> causes severe ALKALINE LIQUEFACTIVE NECROSIS. Can cause full-thickness esophageal perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, or catastrophic AORTO-ESOPHAGEAL FISTULA (fatal exsanguination) WITHIN 2 HOURS! Radiographic hallmarks: on AP view, demonstrates a "HALO SIGN" or "DOUBLE-RING SIGN" (outer ring of negative pole, inner ring of positive pole); on lateral view, demonstrates a distinct "STEP-OFF" at the junction of the poles. DECISIVE MANAGEMENT: IMMEDIATE EMERGENT ENDOSCOPIC REMOVAL WITHIN 2 HOURS. (Oral honey can be given as a temporizing measure to neutralize alkaline generation). 2. ESOPHAGEAL COIN: Smooth, homogeneous density without halo or step-off; if asymptomatic, can be observed for 24 hours to allow spontaneous passage into stomach.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Bacterial Meningitis Dexamethasone Timing and Empiric Coverage
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Bacterial Meningitis: Triad of fever, altered mental status, and nuchal rigidity (positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs). Diagnostic and therapeutic sequence: 1. If no signs of elevated ICP (no papilledema, no focal neurological deficits, normal consciousness, immunocompetent): LUMBAR PUNCTURE FIRST, followed immediately by antibiotics; 2. If signs of elevated ICP or focal deficits: BLOOD CULTURES FIRST, IMMEDIATE EMPIRIC ANTIBIOTICS, then head CT prior to LP; 3. EMPIRIC ANTIBIOTICS: Intravenous VANCOMYCIN PLUS 3RD-GEN CEPHALOSPORIN (CEFTRIAXONE / CEFOTAXIME); ADD AMPICILLIN if age >= 50, immunocompromised, or pregnant (to cover Listeria monocytogenes); 4. ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROIDS: INTRAVENOUS DEXAMETHASONE (10 mg IV) MUST BE ADMINISTERED PRIOR TO OR CONCURRENTLY WITH THE FIRST DOSE OF ANTIBIOTICS. Dexamethasone dampens the intense inflammatory cascade induced by bactericidal lysis, significantly reducing SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS and neurological morbidity in Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis. Discontinue dexamethasone if another pathogen (e.g., Neisseria) is identified.

subject: Medicine
topic: Post-Cardiac Arrest Targeted Temperature Management Protocol
shortestValidSolution: Manage Post-Cardiac Arrest Care after Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC): Patient resuscitated from out-of-hospital or in-hospital cardiac arrest (e.g., ventricular fibrillation) who REMAINS COMATOSE (unresponsive, fails to follow commands). Management protocol: 1. TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT (TTM): Indicated for ALL comatose patients with ROSC. Target a CONSTANT CORE TEMPERATURE BETWEEN 32 C AND 36 C (or strictly maintain < 37.5 C to prevent fever) for at least 24 HOURS, using surface cooling blankets or intravascular catheters. Therapeutic hypothermia decreases cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2 by ~6-8% per 1 C drop), reduces free radical generation, prevents neuronal apoptosis, and mitigates reperfusion injury, improving neurological survival; 2. Emergent Coronary Angiography (cath lab) if STEMI is present on post-ROSC ECG; 3. Avoid hyperoxia (target PaO2 100 mm Hg, SaO2 92-98%) and avoid hypocapnia (keep PaCO2 35-45 mm Hg to prevent cerebral vasoconstriction).

subject: Medicine
topic: Acetaminophen Toxicity Nomogram Timing and N-Acetylcysteine
shortestValidSolution: Manage Toxic Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) Ingestion: Most common cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Pathogenesis: At therapeutic doses, 90% is glucuronidated/sulfated; 5-10% is metabolized by CYP2E1 into N-ACETYL-P-BENZOQUINONE IMINE (NAPQI), a highly toxic reactive intermediate immediately detoxified by hepatic GLUTATHIONE. In overdose, sulfation/glucuronidation pathways are saturated, CYP2E1 shunts massive drug into NAPQI, depleting glutathione. Free NAPQI covalently binds hepatic centrilobular (Zone 3) hepatocytes, causing massive hepatic necrosis. MANAGEMENT TIMELINE: 1. If patient presents < 4 hours after ingestion: Activated charcoal (if < 2 hours) AND DRAW STAT 4-HOUR SERUM ACETAMINOPHEN LEVEL; 2. PLOT ON RUMACK-MATTHEW NOMOGRAM (valid strictly between 4 and 24 hours post-acute ingestion); 3. If serum concentration is ON OR ABOVE THE TREATMENT LINE (150 microg/mL at 4 hours): ADMINISTER N-ACETYLCYSTEINE (NAC) IMMEDIATELY (IV or oral). NAC acts as a glutathione precursor and substitute, completely preventing hepatotoxicity if given within 8 hours. If ingestion time is unknown or presentation is late (> 24 hours) with elevated transaminases, give NAC immediately without waiting for nomograms.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Anaphylaxis Intramuscular Epinephrine Injection Protocol
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Anaphylaxis: severe, life-threatening systemic Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction (antigen cross-links IgE on mast cells/basophils -> massive release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, PAF). Clinical criteria: Involvement of skin/mucosa (urticaria, angioedema, flushing) PLUS AT LEAST ONE OF: 1. Respiratory compromise (stridor, wheezing, bronchospasm, dyspnea); 2. Cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, syncope, shock); or 3. Persistent GI symptoms (cramping, vomiting). FIRST-LINE, LIFE-SAVING DRUG OF CHOICE: INTRAMUSCULAR (IM) EPINEPHRINE (1:1,000 concentration / 1 mg/mL; dose 0.3-0.5 mg in adults, 0.01 mg/kg in children). ROUTE AND SITE OF INJECTION: ANTEROLATERAL THIGH (vastus lateralis muscle). IM thigh injection achieves FASTER AND SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER PEAK PLASMA CONCENTRATIONS than deltoid injection or subcutaneous injection! Epinephrine activates: Alpha-1 (vasoconstriction, reverses hypotension/angioedema), Beta-1 (inotropic/chronotropic), Beta-2 (bronchodilation, shuts off mast cell degranulation via cAMP). Antihistamines and corticosteroids are strictly SECOND-LINE adjunctive agents and must NEVER delay epinephrine!

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Preeclampsia with Severe Features Management at Term vs Preterm
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Preeclampsia with Severe Features: gestational age >= 34 weeks + persistent SBP >= 160 mm Hg or DBP >= 110 mm Hg (or end-organ dysfunction: platelets < 100,000, Cr > 1.1, elevated transaminases, pulmonary edema, or new visual/cerebral symptoms). MANAGEMENT PRIORITY: 1. IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; 2. IV antihypertensives (labetalol, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine) for SBP >= 160 or DBP >= 110; 3. DELIVERY at >= 34 weeks of gestation (expectant management is contraindicated beyond 34 weeks when severe features are present).

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Third-Trimester Vaginal Bleeding Differentiation
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate cause of third-trimester hemorrhage: PAINFUL vaginal bleeding + hypertonic/tender uterus + high-frequency contractions + fetal heart rate decelerations = PLACENTAL ABRUPTION (retroplacental hemorrhage). PAINLESS bright red vaginal bleeding = PLACENTA PREVIA. CRUCIAL CLINICAL RULE: Digital vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated until transabdominal/transvaginal ultrasound excludes placenta previa. In hemodynamically unstable placental abruption or acute fetal distress: immediate emergency cesarean delivery is mandatory.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Ectopic Pregnancy Medical vs Surgical Management Contraindications
shortestValidSolution: Identify contraindications to Methotrexate for Ectopic Pregnancy: 1. Hemodynamic instability; 2. Signs of tubal rupture/hemoperitoneum (peritoneal signs, free fluid in pouch of Douglas/Morison pouch); 3. Gestational mass > 3.5-4 cm; 4. Fetal cardiac activity; 5. Baseline beta-hCG > 5,000 mIU/mL; 6. Pulmonary/renal/hepatic disease. Hemodynamically unstable patient or suspected tubal rupture requires IMMEDIATE EXPLORATORY LAPAROSCOPY (or laparotomy) with salpingectomy.

topic: Postpartum Hemorrhage Algorithmic Uterotonic Sequence

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Preterm Premature Rupture of Membranes Management at 30 Weeks
shortestValidSolution: Manage PPROM < 34 weeks without infection/distress: 1. Latency antibiotics (7-day course: IV ampicillin + erythromycin/azithromycin followed by oral amoxicillin + erythromycin) to prolong latency and reduce chorioamnionitis/neonatal sepsis; 2. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) to accelerate fetal lung maturity; 3. IV Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection if < 32 weeks; 4. GBS prophylaxis if in active labor. Delivery is indicated at 34 weeks or immediately if chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise develops.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis Resuscitation Priorities
shortestValidSolution: Manage Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Non-bilious projectile vomiting in a 3-6 week-old infant with "olive-shaped" epigastric mass. Labs show HYPOCHLOREMIC, HYPOKALEMIC METABOLIC ALKALOSIS (due to loss of HCl from vomiting and renal compensation retaining H+ in exchange for K+). CRITICAL CLINICAL RULE: Pyloromyotomy is NEVER an emergency. OPERATIVE CORRECTION MUST BE DELAYED UNTIL COMPLETE CORRECTION OF DEHYDRATION AND ELECTROLYTE/ACID-BASE DISTURBANCES (normal chloride, potassium, and serum bicarbonate < 28-30 mEq/L) to prevent life-threatening intraoperative apnea and cardiac arrhythmias.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Intussusception Diagnostic and Therapeutic Approach
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Ileocolic Intussusception: infant/toddler (6-36 months) with episodic severe crampy abdominal pain (inconsolable crying with legs drawn up to chest), vomiting, and classic "currant-jelly" stool or right upper quadrant sausage-shaped mass (empty RLQ - Dance sign). Ultrasound confirms: "target" or "donut" sign. MANAGEMENT: 1. If NO peritonitis or bowel perforation: PNEUMATIC (AIR-CONTRAST) OR HYDROSTATIC ENEMA is both diagnostic and therapeutic (success > 80-90%). 2. If PERITONITIS, PERFORATION, OR PERSISTENT REFRACTORY ILEUS: IMMEDIATE SURGICAL LAPAROTOMY is mandatory.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Simple vs Complex Febrile Seizures Evaluation
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Febrile Seizures: - SIMPLE FEBRILE SEIZURE: Generalized tonic-clonic, duration < 15 minutes, occurs only ONCE in 24 hours, normal baseline neurological status, child age 6 months to 5 years. Management: REASSURANCE, education, antipyretics for comfort (does not prevent seizure recurrence), NO routine LP, EEG, or neuroimaging unless meningeal signs or persistent altered mental status are present. - COMPLEX: Focal onset, duration >= 15 min, or recurrent within 24 hours (requires workup).

distractorExclusion: Lumbar puncture is not indicated in a fully immunized child who presents with a simple febrile seizure, has returned to normal mental status, and demonstrates no meningeal signs.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Imaging Modalities
shortestValidSolution: Evaluate Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH): Risk factors: breech presentation, female sex, family history. Physical exam: positive Barlow (dislocates hip) or Ortolani (reduces hip with "clunk"), asymmetric gluteal/inguinal folds. IMAGING CHOICE DEPENDS ON AGE: - AGE < 4-6 MONTHS: ULTRASOUND OF THE HIPS (femoral head is cartilaginous and radiolucent on X-ray); - AGE >= 4-6 MONTHS: ANTEROPOSTERIOR HIP RADIOGRAPHY (femoral head ossification center is visible). Treatment < 6 months: Pavlik harness.

topic: Pertussis Diagnostic Testing and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
shortestValidSolution: Manage Bordetella pertussis (Whooping Cough): Clinical phases: 1. Catarrhal (mild rhinorrhea/cough); 2. Paroxysmal (severe coughing fits with inspiratory whoop and posttussive emesis/syncope); 3. Convalescent. Classic lab finding: MARKED LYMPHOCYTOSIS. Diagnosis: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR/culture. MANAGEMENT PRIORITY: 1. Treat patient with MACROLIDE (AZITHROMYCIN or clarithromycin) to reduce transmission; 2. POST-EXPOSURE ANTIMICROBIAL PROPHYLAXIS WITH ORAL AZITHROMYCIN FOR ALL CLOSE/HOUSEHOLD CONTACTS REGARDLESS OF VACCINATION STATUS (due to waning acellular vaccine immunity).

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Salicylate Toxicity Pathophysiology and Management
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Acute Salicylate (Aspirin) Toxicity: - Classic early symptom: TINNITUS, nausea, tachypnea/hyperpnea, diaphoresis. - ACID-BASE HALLMARK: MIXED PRIMARY RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS (direct medullary respiratory center stimulation) AND HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation accumulating lactic acid and ketoacids). Near-normal pH with low PaCO2 and very low HCO3 confirms mixed disorder. - MANAGEMENT: 1. IV fluid resuscitation; 2. URINARY ALKALINIZATION WITH INTRAVENOUS SODIUM BICARBONATE (ion-trapping: traps charged salicylate in urine, accelerating excretion and preventing CNS entry); 3. Hemodialysis if serum salicylate > 90-100 mg/dL, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or refractory acidosis.

subject: Medicine
topic: Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose Electrocardiogram Abnormalities
shortestValidSolution: Recognize TCA Overdose (amitriptyline, nortriptyline): 1. Anticholinergic toxidrome (hyperthermia, mydriasis, flushed dry skin, delirium, urinary retention); 2. CNS toxicity (seizures, coma); 3. CARDIOVASCULAR TOXICITY (hypotension and VENTRICULAR DYSRHYTHMIAS due to myocardial fast sodium channel blockade). ECG FINDINGS: QRS PROLONGATION (> 100 ms predicts seizures, > 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias), right axis deviation, terminal R wave > 3 mm in aVR. TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS SODIUM BICARBONATE (increases extracellular Na+ gradient and elevates serum pH, dissociating the drug from cardiac sodium channels).

topic: Organophosphate and Carbamate Poisoning Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Organophosphate Toxicity (irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition leading to acetylcholine excess): - MUSCARINIC TOXIDROME (DUMBBELLS: Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhea/Bronchospasm/Bradycardia, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation). Killer "Bs": Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, Bradycardia. - NICOTINIC SYMPTOMS: Muscle fasciculations, weakness, diaphragmatic paralysis. - IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: 1. PPE/Decontamination; 2. ATROPINE FIRST (competitive muscarinic antagonist; titrate until pulmonary secretions clear and bronchospasm resolves); 3. PRALIDOXIME (2-PAM) SECOND (regenerates acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors before "aging" occurs).

topic: Toxic Alcohol Ingestion Differentiation and Treatment
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Toxic Alcohols: Both present with HIGH OSMOLAL GAP and HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS. - ETHYLENE GLYCOL: Metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to GLYCOLIC ACID and OXALIC ACID -> ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY, flank pain, and ENVELOPE-SHAPED CALCIUM OXALATE CRYSTALS in urine (positive Wood lamp fluorescence). - METHANOL: Metabolized to FORMIC ACID -> OPTIC PAPILLITIS, "snowfield" visual loss, and retinal edema. - TREATMENT FOR BOTH: 1. FOMEPIZOLE (competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite generation); 2. HEMODIALYSIS for severe refractory acidosis (pH < 7.25), renal failure, vision loss, or level > 50 mg/dL.

subject: Medicine
topic: Carbon Monoxide vs Cyanide Poisoning Differentiation
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Enclosed Space Fire Inhalation Toxins: - CARBON MONOXIDE (CO): Binds hemoglobin with 200x affinity of O2 (carboxyhemoglobin), shifting O2-Hb curve left. Standard pulse oximetry is FALSELY NORMAL. Symptoms: headache, malaise, confusion, pink skin (rare). Diagnosis: CO-oximetry (elevated carboxyhemoglobin). TREATMENT: 100% NORMOBARIC O2; HYPERBARIC O2 (HBO) if COHb > 25% (or > 15% in pregnancy), loss of consciousness, neurological deficits, or cardiac ischemia. - CYANIDE: Blocks complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), causing cellular asphyxiation and SEVERE LACTIC ACIDOSIS (lactate > 8-10 mmol/L). Treatment: HYDROXOCOBALAMIN.

strongestDistractor: Intravenous administration of hydroxocobalamin infusion
distractorExclusion: Hydroxocobalamin is the antidote for cyanide poisoning (which typically causes profound lactic acidosis > 8-10 mmol/L and cardiovascular collapse); here lactate is only mildly elevated (3.1) and COHb is 32% with myocardial ischemia, making hyperbaric oxygen the priority.

subject: Medicine
topic: Methemoglobinemia Etiology and Methylene Blue Reversal
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Methemoglobinemia: Triggered by oxidizing agents (topical local anesthetics: BENZOCAINE spray, lidocaine; DAPSONE; nitrates). Fe2+ (ferrous) is oxidized to Fe3+ (ferric), which cannot bind O2. Hallmark: "CHOCOLATE-COLORED BLOOD", cyanosis unresponsive to 100% supplemental O2, and "PULSE OXIMETRY SATURATION GAP" (pulse oximeter stuck around ~85% while arterial blood gas shows normal PaO2). TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS METHYLENE BLUE (acts as electron acceptor for NADPH-methemoglobin reductase). CAUTION: Methylene blue is CONTRAINDICATED in patients with G6PD DEFICIENCY (causes severe hemolysis because NADPH is deficient; treat with IV ascorbic acid instead).

distractorExclusion: Benzocaine allergy or angioedema causes swelling of the tongue and airway obstruction with stridor, not refractory cyanosis with dark brown blood and normal breath sounds.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Acute Iron Poisoning Clinical Phases and Chelation
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Iron Toxicity (pediatric ingestion of prenatal vitamins / iron supplements): - PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Free iron generates toxic hydroxyl free radicals, causing direct mucosal corrosion, severe hypovolemic shock, and mitochondrial damage. - CLINICAL STAGES: 1. GI stage (0-6 hours: abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena); 2. Latent quiescent stage (6-24 hours); 3. Shock/Metabolic acidosis stage (12-48 hours: severe lactic acidosis, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy); 4. Hepatic failure (2-3 days); 5. Bowel obstruction (2-6 weeks: gastric outlet/pyloric scarring). - DIAGNOSIS: Radiopaque pills on abdominal X-ray, high serum iron (> 350-500 mcg/dL). - TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS DEFEROXAMINE (chelates ferric iron to form ferrioxamine, excreted in urine turning it "vin rosé" reddish-pink).

subject: Medicine
topic: Lead Poisoning Clinical Recognition and Chelation Indications
shortestValidSolution: Manage Lead Poisoning (plumbism): Exposure in workers (battery, foundry, demolition) or children (lead paint in pre-1978 homes). Symptoms: "LEAD" - Leads (lines on gingiva: Burton lines; and metaphyses on X-ray), Encephalopathy (irritability, memory loss, foot/wrist drop due to peripheral neuropathy), Abdominal colic (lead colic), Microcytic sideroblastic/hemolytic Anemia with BASOPHILIC STIPPLING. CHELATION GUIDELINES: - Asymptomatic mild blood lead level (BLL) < 45 mcg/dL in children: Environmental removal and nutritional counseling; - BLL 45-69 mcg/dL: Oral SUCCIMER (DMSA); - Severe toxicity BLL >= 70 mcg/dL or encephalopathy: INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM DISODIUM EDTA + INTRAMUSCULAR DIMERCAPROL (BAL).

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia Evaluation and Phototherapy Thresholds
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia: 1. UNCONJUGATED (INDIRECT) HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA: Risk of BIND (bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction) / KERNICTERUS (basal ganglia/brainstem deposition). Jaundice within FIRST 24 HOURS is ALWAYS PATHOLOGIC (most commonly ABO or Rh hemolytic disease). Manage based on nomograms: INTENSIVE PHOTOTHERAPY; if total serum bilirubin (TSB) approaches/exceeds exchange threshold (e.g. >= 20-25 mg/dL depending on hours of life and neurotoxicity risk factors) or signs of encephalopathy: IMMEDIATE EXCHANGE TRANSFUSION. 2. CONJUGATED (DIRECT > 20% of TSB): Biliary atresia (pale stools, dark urine; requires Kasai procedure).

shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Epiglottitis (Haemophilus influenzae type b or Streptococcus/Staphylococcus): Presentation: Rapidly progressive high fever, severe sore throat, "3 Ds" (Drooling, Dysphagia, Distress), tripod position with neck hyperextended. X-ray shows "thumbprint sign" (do NOT obtain if patient in distress). CRITICAL AIRWAY RULE: MINIMIZE AGITATION. DO NOT EXAMINE OROPHARYNX WITH TONGUE DEPRESSOR OR ATTEMPT AWAKE INTUBATION IN ED (triggers fatal laryngospasm). IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: TRANSPORT DIRECTLY TO OPERATING ROOM WITH ANESTHESIOLOGY AND ENT FOR CONTROLLED ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION under inhalational anesthesia, followed by IV ceftriaxone + vancomycin.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Pediatric Ingestion of Button Batteries vs Blunt Foreign Bodies
shortestValidSolution: Manage Foreign Body Ingestion (Button Battery vs Coin): - Radiographic differentiation: BUTTON BATTERY shows "DOUBLE-RING" OR "HALO" SIGN on AP view and "STEP-OFF" on lateral view. COIN shows homogeneous single density with smooth border. - ESOPHAGEAL BUTTON BATTERY IS A SURGICAL EMERGENCY: Generates local electrical current causing rapid liquefactive necrosis, esophageal perforation, and tracheoesophageal or aortoenteric fistula within 2 HOURS. subject: Pediatrics
topic: Acute Bacterial Meningitis in Children Empiric Regimen and Adjuncts
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Bacterial Meningitis in Children (> 1 month old: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis): - EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN: IV VANCOMYCIN + CEFTRIAXONE (or Cefotaxime). - ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROIDS: INTRAVENOUS DEXAMETHASONE given PRIOR TO OR CONCURRENTLY WITH the first dose of antibiotics. Mechanism: Dampens the intense inflammatory cascade triggered by antibiotic-induced bacterial lysis in the subarachnoid space; significantly reduces the incidence of SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS and neurological sequelae (especially with S. pneumoniae and Hib). Giving steroids after antibiotics shows no clinical benefit.

subject: Medicine
topic: Post-Cardiac Arrest Targeted Temperature Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Post-Cardiac Arrest Care after Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC): In comatose patients (not following commands): 1. TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT (TTM): Maintain a constant core body temperature between 32°C and 36°C (or strict fever prevention < 37.5°C) for at least 24 hours. Mechanism: Lowers cerebral metabolic demand, suppresses free radical generation, and inhibits ischemic neuronal apoptosis, significantly improving neurological recovery. 2. AVOID FEVER (> 37.7°C), which exacerbates secondary brain injury. 3. Immediate coronary angiography for STEMI or suspected coronary etiology. 4. Avoid hyperoxia and hypocapnia.

subject: Medicine
topic: Acute Ischemic Stroke Thrombolysis Eligibility and Blood Pressure Goals
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Ischemic Stroke: Window for IV Alteplase (or Tenecteplase) is < 4.5 hours from last known normal. CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATIONS: Intracranial hemorrhage on non-contrast CT, ischemic stroke or severe head trauma within past 3 months, major surgery within 14 days, active internal bleeding, platelet count < 100,000, INR > 1.7 or therapeutic DOAC use, and BLOOD PRESSURE >= 185/110 mm Hg REFRACTORY TO TREATMENT. Management of high BP: Administer IV LABETALOL OR NICARDIPINE to lower BP < 185/110 BEFORE thrombolytic infusion; maintain BP < 180/105 during and for 24 hours post-infusion.

subject: Medicine
topic: Status Epilepticus First- and Second-Line Pharmacotherapy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Convulsive Status Epilepticus (continuous seizure >= 5 minutes or >= 2 seizures without full recovery of consciousness between): - FIRST-LINE EMERGENCE (0-10 min): INTRAVENOUS LORAZEPAM (or IM Midazolam if no IV access). - SECOND-LINE URGENT CONTROL (10-30 min): NON-SEDATING ANTISEIZURE MEDICATION (IV LEVETIRACETAM, FOSPHENYTOIN, or SODIUM VALPROATE). - REFRACTORY STATUS (> 30 min): Continuous general anesthetic infusion (PROPOFOL, MIDAZOLAM, or PENTOBARBITAL) with endotracheal intubation and continuous EEG monitoring.

subject: Medicine
topic: Myasthenic Crisis Respiratory Failure and Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Myasthenic Crisis (severe exacerbation of generalized myasthenia gravis with diaphragmatic/bulbar weakness): - MONITORING FOR IMPENDING RESPIRATORY FAILURE: Serial forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF). INTUBATE IF: FVC < 15-20 mL/kg or NIF worse than -20 to -30 cm H2O ("20/30 rule"), or severe bulbar weakness with aspiration risk. - DEFINITIVE TREATMENT: PLASMAPHERESIS (PLEX) OR INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN (IVIG) + systemic corticosteroids. - CRITICAL MEDICATION ADJUSTMENT: TEMPORARILY WITHHOLD PYRIDOSTIGMINE (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) during mechanical ventilation to eliminate excessive bronchorrhea and airway secretions that impair extubation.

subject: Medicine
topic: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Medical and Surgical Priorities
shortestValidSolution: Manage Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH, ruptured saccular/berry aneurysm): Diagnosis: Non-contrast head CT (high sensitivity in first 6 hours); if negative and clinical suspicion high: LUMBAR PUNCTURE (shows xanthochromia and persistently elevated RBCs from tube 1 to tube 4). IMMEDIATE COMPREHENSIVE MANAGEMENT: 1. SECURE ANEURYSM EARLY (< 24-72 hours via endovascular coiling or surgical clipping) to prevent catastrophic REBLEEDING (greatest risk in first 24 hours); 2. NIMODIPINE (oral calcium channel blocker) started immediately to prevent DELAYED CEREBRAL ISCHEMIA / VASOSPASM (peaks at days 3-14); 3. Blood pressure control (maintain SBP < 140-160 mm Hg prior to securing aneurysm).

subject: Medicine
topic: Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis Immediate Glucocorticoid Therapy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis (GCA / Horton disease): Granulomatous large/medium-vessel vasculitis in patients >= 50 years old. Symptoms: New unilateral headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica (proximal stiffness), markedly elevated ESR (> 50-100 mm/hr) and CRP. Most feared complication: PERMANENT BLINDNESS due to ischemic optic neuropathy (ophthalmic/posterior ciliary artery occlusion). GOLDEN CLINICAL RULE: NEVER DELAY SYSTEMIC CORTICOSTEROIDS TO AWAIT TEMPORAL ARTERY BIOPSY. Immediate high-dose oral prednisone (or IV methylprednisolone if vision loss has begun) must be started IMMEDIATELY, followed by biopsy within 1-2 weeks (pathology remains positive for weeks).

subject: Medicine
topic: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus Diagnosis and Treatment
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH, impaired CSF absorption across arachnoid villi): - CLASSIC CLINICAL TRIAD: "WET, WACKY, WOBBLY" - 1. Gait disturbance (earliest and most responsive to treatment: broad-based, slow, shuffling, "magnetic" gait as if feet are glued to floor); 2. Urinary incontinence (urgency/frequency progressing to overt incontinence); 3. Cognitive impairment / dementia. - NEUROIMAGING: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cerebral sulcal atrophy (Evans index > 0.3). - CONFIRMATORY DIAGNOSTIC TEST: HIGH-VOLUME LUMBAR PUNCTURE (tap test: removal of 30-50 mL CSF) demonstrating OBJECTIVE IMPROVEMENT IN GAIT SPEED AND STRIDE LENGTH. - DEFINITIVE TREATMENT: VENTRICULOPERITONEAL (VP) SHUNT.

distractorExclusion: Although gait is impaired, the absence of resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, or asymmetric bradykinesia—combined with ventriculomegaly and urinary incontinence—rules out Parkinson disease; dopaminergic therapy is ineffective.

subject: Medicine
topic: Wernicke Encephalopathy Recognition and Sequence of Vitamin Repletion
shortestValidSolution: Manage Wernicke Encephalopathy: Acute thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically in chronic alcohol use disorder, malabsorption, or bariatric surgery. CLASSIC TRIAD: 1. ENCEPHALOPATHY (confusion, disorientation, apathy); 2. OCULOMOTOR DYSFUNCTION (horizontal nystagmus, bilateral abducens [CN VI] palsy, conjugate gaze palsy); 3. GAIT ATAXIA (wide-based cerebellar ataxia). PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Thiamine is a required cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. If dextrose is given without thiamine, glucose metabolism rapidly exhausts residual thiamine stores, causing acute metabolic neuronal necrosis in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal gray. GOLDEN RULE: ADMINISTER HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS THIAMINE BEFORE OR CONCURRENTLY WITH INTRAVENOUS DEXTROSE.

distractorExclusion: Infusing dextrose alone in a thiamine-deficient patient rapidly exhausts remaining cofactor stores, converting reversible Wernicke encephalopathy into permanent Korsakoff syndrome.

subject: Medicine
topic: Guillain-Barré Syndrome Monitoring and Immunotherapy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy - AIDP): Post-infectious autoimmune molecular mimicry (Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV). Symptoms: ASCENDING, SYMMETRICAL FLACCID WEAKNESS with HYPOREFLEXIA OR AREFLEXIA, autonomic dysfunction. CSF: ALBUMINOCYTOLOGIC DISSOCIATION (elevated protein with normal WBC). CRITICAL MONITORING: SERIAL BEDSIDE SPIROMETRY (Forced Vital Capacity [FVC] and Negative Inspiratory Force [NIF]) every 4-6 hours to anticipate diaphragmatic paralysis. INTUBATE if FVC < 15-20 mL/kg or NIF worse than -30 cm H2O. TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN (IVIG) OR PLASMAPHERESIS (PLEX). STRICTLY INEFFECTIVE: Corticosteroids (no benefit in GBS).

topic: Herpes Simplex Encephalitis Clinical Features and Immediate Empiric Antiviral
shortestValidSolution: Manage Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) Encephalitis: - CLINICAL PICTURE: Acute onset of fever, headache, altered mental status, bizarre behavioral changes/hallucinations, and focal seizures. - PATHOLOGY/IMAGING: Predilection for INFEROMEDIAL TEMPORAL LOBES (and orbitofrontal cortex), showing edema, hemorrhage, and periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) on EEG. - CSF FINDINGS: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and ELEVATED ERYTHROCYTES (RBCs) without xanthochromia (due to hemorrhagic temporal lobe necrotizing encephalitis). PCR confirms HSV DNA. - MANAGEMENT PRIORITY: IMMEDIATE EMPIRIC INTRAVENOUS ACYCLOVIR. NEVER DELAY ACYCLOVIR PENDING LUMBAR PUNCTURE OR PCR RESULTS (mortality exceeds 70% if untreated).

subject: Surgery
topic: Epidural Hematoma Anatomy and Emergency Surgical Decompression
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Epidural Hematoma (EDH): - ANATOMY: Fracture of the PTERION (thinnest part of skull where frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet) lacerating the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY (branch of maxillary artery). - CLINICAL COURSE: Classic "LUCID INTERVAL" (initial loss of consciousness from concussion -> temporary regaining of consciousness -> rapid deterioration into coma as arterial hematoma expands). Signs of UNCAL HERNIATION: ipsilateral dilated, fixed pupil (CN III compression) and contralateral hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle compression). - CT HEAD: BICONVEX (LENTICULAR) HYPERDENSITY that DOES NOT CROSS SUTURE LINES (limited by dura attached to sutures). - TREATMENT: IMMEDIATE EMERGENT SURGICAL CRANIOTOMY AND HEMATOMA EVACUATION.

subject: Medicine
topic: Tumor Lysis Syndrome Prevention and Rasburicase Mechanism
shortestValidSolution: Manage Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS): Massive release of intracellular contents following induction chemotherapy for high-turnover hematologic malignancies (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, AML). - LAB ABNORMALITIES: HYPERKALEMIA (arrhythmias), HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA (calcium-phosphate precipitation), HYPOCALCEMIA (tetany, seizures), and HYPERURICEMIA (uric acid nephropathy/AKI). - MANAGEMENT: 1. Aggressive IV hydration (isotonic saline); 2. ALLOPURINOL (xanthine oxidase inhibitor, PREVENTS new uric acid formation, best for low-to-intermediate risk); 3. RASBURICASE (recombinant urate oxidase that BREAKS DOWN EXISTING URIC ACID into allantoin, highly soluble and readily excreted; INDICATED FOR HIGH RISK OR ESTABLISHED HYPERURICEMIA). CAUTION: Rasburicase is CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD DEFICIENCY (causes severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia).

subject: Medicine
topic: Malignant Epidural Spinal Cord Compression Emergency Protocol
shortestValidSolution: Manage Malignant Epidural Spinal Cord Compression (MESCC): True oncologic emergency (prostate, breast, lung cancer, myeloma, renal cell carcinoma). - CLINICAL PROGRESSION: 1. Progressive, severe, focal back pain (worse lying flat, worse with percussion/valsalva); 2. Motor weakness (lower extremity weakness, difficulty walking); 3. Sensory level loss; 4. Autonomic/sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention with overflow incontinence, fecal incontinence - late finding, poor prognosis for recovery). - EMERGENCY PROTOCOL: 1. IMMEDIATE HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS DEXAMETHASONE (reduces vasogenic spinal cord edema, relieves pain, and preserves neurologic function); 2. URGENT MRI OF THE ENTIRE SPINE (scans cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine because multi-level metastases occur in ~30%); 3. Emergency radiation oncology and neurosurgical spine consultation for decompression.

subject: Medicine
topic: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome Diagnosis and Initial Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome: Extrinsic compression or intravascular thrombosis of the thin-walled SVC by mediastinal malignancy (small cell lung carcinoma, non-small cell lung carcinoma, lymphoma) or indwelling central venous catheter/pacemaker lead. - SYMPTOMS: Facial fullness/edema, bilateral arm swelling, neck vein distention, dilated subcutaneous collateral veins across upper chest wall, dyspnea, and plethora (worse leaning forward - Pemberton sign). - DIAGNOSIS: CONTRAST-ENHANCED CT SCAN OF THE CHEST. - MANAGEMENT: 1. Elevation of head of bed and supplemental oxygen; 2. Intravenous corticosteroids for lymphoma or thymoma; 3. ENDOVASCULAR STENTING (rapid symptomatic relief) or radiation therapy / systemic chemotherapy based on tumor histology.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Hypercalcemia of Malignancy Management Hierarchy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Severe Hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 14 mg/dL or symptomatic): Classically caused by malignancy (PTHrP from squamous cell cancers; bone osteolytic metastases in breast cancer/myeloma; or 1,25-(OH)2D production in lymphoma). Symptoms: "Stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric overtones" + severe volume depletion (nephrogenic DI). SHORT-TERM & LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL: 1. IMMEDIATE AGGRESSIVE INTRAVENOUS ISOTONIC SALINE (replaces massive volume deficits and promotes calciuresis); 2. CALCITONIN (subcutaneous/IM: fast-acting within 4-6 hours by inhibiting osteoclasts, but causes tachyphylaxis after 48 hours); 3. INTRAVENOUS BISPHOSPHONATES (ZOLEDRONIC ACID or pamidronate: potent osteoclast inhibitors that take 48-72 hours to work but provide sustained control for weeks). 4. AVOID FUROSEMIDE unless volume overload develops.

topic: Neutropenic Fever Empiric Antimicrobial Regimen Selection
shortestValidSolution: Manage Febrile Neutropenia: - DEFINITION: Single oral temperature >= 38.3°C (101.0°F) or >= 38.0°C (100.4°F) sustained for >= 1 hour in a patient with ABSOLUTE NEUTROPHIL COUNT (ANC) < 500/mm³ (or expected to fall < 500 within 48 hours). - PATHOGENESIS: Translocation of endogenous flora across mucositis breakdown; Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes rapid sepsis and mortality within hours. - INITIAL THERAPY: IMMEDIATE IV ANTIPSEUDOMONAL MONOTHERAPY: CEFEPIME, PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM, OR MEROPENEM. - INDICATIONS TO ADD VANCOMYCIN: Hemodynamic instability/shock, catheter-related infection, skin/soft tissue infection, pneumonia, or MRSA colonization. Do NOT add vancomycin routinely without these indications.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Pathophysiology and Treatment
shortestValidSolution: Manage Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS): Triggered by DOPAMINE D2 RECEPTOR ANTAGONISTS (high-potency typical antipsychotics like haloperidol, fluphenazine; or abrupt withdrawal of dopamine agonists like levodopa). TETRAD OF FEATURES: 1. "LEAD-PIPE" GENERALIZED MUSCLE RIGIDITY; 2. HYPERTHERMIA (temp often > 40°C / 104°F); 3. AUTONOMIC INSTABILITY (tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis); 4. ALTERED MENTAL STATUS (delirium, stupor, mutism). LABS: Markedly elevated CREATINE KINASE (CK > 1,000-50,000 U/L) and LEUKOCYTOSIS. TREATMENT: 1. Discontinue offending neuroleptic; 2. Aggressive cooling & IV hydration (prevent myoglobinuric renal failure); 3. DANTROLENE (ryanodine receptor blocker, relaxes muscle) or BROMOCRIPTINE (dopamine agonist).

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Serotonin Syndrome vs Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Serotonin Syndrome (SS) from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS): - SS TRIGGER: Combinations of serotonergic agents (SSRI/SNRI + MAOI, tramadol, linezolid, triptan, dextromethorphan, MDMA). - CLINICAL HALLMARK: NEUROMUSCULAR EXCITATION (HYPERREFLEXIA, SPONTANEOUS/INDUCIBLE CLONUS, OCULAR CLONUS, TREMOR), agitation, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds (diarrhea), and hyperthermia. Hunter criteria: Clonus is the most sensitive finding. - CONTRAST WITH NMS: NMS has "lead-pipe" rigidity, hyporeflexia, and normal/hypoactive bowel sounds. - TREATMENT FOR SS: 1. Discontinue serotonergic agents; 2. IV Benzodiazepines (sedation, reduce agitation/hyperthermia); 3. CYPROHEPTADINE (5-HT2A serotonin receptor antagonist) for moderate-to-severe cases.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Acute Dystonic Reaction Diagnosis and Treatment
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Dystonic Reaction (extrapyramidal symptom [EPS] occurring within hours to days of starting dopamine D2 antagonists): - AGENTS: High-potency first-generation antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine). - CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS: Sudden, involuntary, painful, sustained muscle contractions: TORTICOLLIS (twisted neck), OCULOGYRIC CRISIS (sustained upward deviation of eyes), TRISMUS (jaw clenching), or OPISTHOTONOS. - PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute disruption of dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia (excess cholinergic activity). - TREATMENT: IMMEDIATE INTRAMUSCULAR OR INTRAVENOUS ANTICHOLINERGIC AGENT: BENZTROPINE OR DIPHENHYDRAMINE (rapid symptom reversal within minutes).

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Lithium Toxicity Manifestations and Hemodialysis Thresholds
shortestValidSolution: Manage Lithium Toxicity: Narrow therapeutic window (0.6-1.2 mEq/L). - PRECIPITATING TRIGGERS: Dehydration, low-sodium diet, or medications that decrease renal clearance: THIAZIDE DIURETICS (highest risk: induces proximal tubular reabsorption of Na+ and Li+), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs. - CLINICAL STAGES: Mild (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fine tremor); Moderate (confusion, lethargy, COARSE TREMOR, dysarthria, ataxia); Severe (seizures, stupor, coma, non-convulsive status, arrhythmias). - TREATMENT: 1. Discontinue lithium + aggressive IV isotonic saline (promotes renal excretion); 2. HEMODIALYSIS INDICATIONS: Serum lithium > 4.0 mEq/L regardless of symptoms, OR serum lithium > 2.5 mEq/L with severe neurologic symptoms (seizures, coma) or renal failure.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens) Protocol
shortestValidSolution: Manage Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome: - TIMELINE: 1. Mild withdrawal (6-12 hr: tremors, insomnia, anxiety, diaphoresis); 2. Withdrawal seizures (12-48 hr: generalized tonic-clonic); 3. Alcoholic hallucinosis (12-48 hr: auditory/visual hallucinations with CLEAR SENSORIUM/intact orientation); 4. DELIRIUM TREMENS (DTs, 48-96 hr: DISORIENTATION/DELIRIUM, severe autonomic hyperactivity: fever, hypertension, drenching diaphoresis, tachycardia). - GOLD STANDARD TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS BENZODIAZEPINES (Diazepam, Chlordiazepoxide, or LORAZEPAM/OXAZEPAM in patients with advanced liver disease/cirrhosis because "LOT" drugs undergo direct glucuronidation without hepatic oxidation). Dose titrated via validated CIWA-Ar protocol.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor Hypertensive Crisis Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage MAOI-Tyramine Hypertensive Crisis: Patient on MONOAMINE OXIDASE INHIBITOR (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, or selegiline) ingests TYRAMINE-RICH FOODS (aged cheeses, cured meats, draft beer, red wine, fava beans, fermented soy). Mechanism: MAO-A in GI tract normally breaks down dietary tyramine. Unmetabolized tyramine enters systemic circulation, gets taken up into sympathetic presynaptic terminals, and forces massive release of NOREPINEPHRINE. Manifestations: Severe occipital headache, profuse sweating, dilated pupils, and MALIGNANT HYPERTENSION (BP > 180/120 mm Hg) risking stroke or aortic dissection. TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS PHENTOLAMINE (non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic blocker) or NITROPRUSSIDE.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Clozapine-Induced Agranulocytosis Monitoring and Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Clozapine-Induced Agranulocytosis: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic indicated for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and reducing suicide risk. SEVERE ADVERSE EFFECT: AGRANULOCYTOSIS (occurs in ~1% of patients, highest in first 6 months). MANDATORY MONITORING: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) weekly for 6 months, every 2 weeks for 6 months, then monthly. CRITICAL ANC ACTION THRESHOLDS: 1. Normal ANC >= 1500/mm³: Continue clozapine; 2. Mild neutropenia (ANC 1000-1499): Continue therapy, monitor ANC 3x/week; 3. SEVERE NEUTROPENIA / AGRANULOCYTOSIS (ANC < 1000, and specifically < 500/mm³): IMMEDIATELY AND PERMANENTLY DISCONTINUE CLOZAPINE. Admit, obtain infectious workup, and NEVER rechallenge.

strongestDistractor: Reduce the clozapine dose by 50% and repeat the complete blood count in 48 hours
distractorExclusion: Dose reduction is completely inadequate; continuing clozapine in the setting of ANC 240/mm³ leads to fulminant septic shock and death.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Acute Catatonia Diagnosis and Lorazepam Challenge
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Catatonia: Neuropsychiatric syndrome occurring in mood disorders (bipolar, major depression) or psychotic disorders. - CLINICAL SIGNS (Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale): MUTISM, STUPOR, CATALEPSY (passive induction of a posture held against gravity), WAXY FLEXIBILITY (slight resistance to repositioning like bending a candle), NEGATIVISM (active resistance to instructions), ECHOLALIA, ECHOPRAXIA. - DIAGNOSTIC & INITIAL THERAPY: LORAZEPAM CHALLENGE TEST (1-2 mg IV lorazepam produces marked temporary relief of catatonic signs within 10-15 minutes, confirming diagnosis). - DEFINITIVE TREATMENT: Scheduled high-dose LORAZEPAM; if refractory or malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability): ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY (ECT). AVOID ANTIPSYCHOTICS (worsens catatonia and precipitates NMS).

AVOID ANTIPSYCHOTICS (worsens catatonia and precipitates NMS).
strongestDistractor: Administer intramuscular haloperidol to manage severe psychotic immobility
distractorExclusion: Antipsychotics such as haloperidol are strictly contraindicated in acute catatonia because dopamine D2 blockade markedly worsens catatonic symptoms and precipitates fatal malignant catatonia or NMS.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Acute Severe Agitation in the Emergency Department
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Severe Agitation and Violent Behavior: Sequence of escalation: 1. Environmental de-escalation (calm verbal engagement, offering oral medication); 2. If verbal de-escalation FAILS and patient poses an IMMEDIATE PHYSICAL THREAT to self or medical staff: RAPID CHEMICAL RESTRAINT. - FIRST-LINE PARENTERAL REGIMEN: INTRAMUSCULAR FIRST-GENERATION ANTIPSYCHOTIC (HALOPERIDOL 5 mg) PLUS INTRAMUSCULAR BENZODIAZEPINE (LORAZEPAM 2 mg) - the classic "5 and 2" combo. (Alternatively: IM Olanzapine or Ziprasidone; DO NOT CO-ADMINISTER IM OLANZAPINE WITH IM BENZODIAZEPINE due to fatal respiratory depression and hypotension).

subject: Geriatrics
topic: Delirium vs Dementia Differentiation and Non-Pharmacologic Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Delirium from Dementia: - DELIRIUM: ACUTE onset (hours to days), FLUCTUATING course, impaired ATTENTION / AWARENESS (cannot spell "WORLD" backward or name months in reverse), altered level of consciousness, visual hallucinations; reversible once underlying medical cause (infection/UTI, electrolyte abnormality, medication change, hypoxia, urinary retention) is treated. - DEMENTIA: Insidious onset (months to years), progressive decline, stable attention in early stages, clear consciousness. - MANAGEMENT OF DELIRIUM: 1. Identify and treat underlying medical trigger; 2. NON-PHARMACOLOGIC PROTOCOLS (reorientation, day-night lighting, frequent mobilization, family presence, sensory aids like glasses/hearing aids); 3. AVOID BENZODIAZEPINES (paradoxically worsens delirium and prolongs hospitalization; only indicated if alcohol/sedative withdrawal).

subject: Surgery
topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome Recognition and Fasciotomy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Acute Compartment Syndrome: High pressure within an osteofascial compartment compromising capillary perfusion and leading to muscle/nerve ischemia. CLASSIC EARLY FINDING: SEVERE PAIN DISPROPORTIONATE TO INJURY and PAIN WITH PASSIVE STRETCH OF COMPARTMENT MUSCLES. Late findings: Paresthesias, pallor, paralysis, pulselessness (sign of irreversible necrosis). DIAGNOSIS: Delta pressure (Diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) <= 30 mm Hg. IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: Bivalve/remove any tight casts or dressings, keep limb at heart level (DO NOT ELEVATE, which worsens perfusion), and perform IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY SURGICAL FASCIOTOMY.

distractorExclusion: Elevating the extremity drops arterial perfusion pressure across the high-pressure compartment, dangerously worsening tissue ischemia and accelerating muscle necrosis.

subject: Surgery
topic: Scaphoid Fracture Management with Negative Initial Radiographs
shortestValidSolution: Manage Suspected Scaphoid Fracture: Fall onto outstretched hand (FOOSH). Physical exam: POINT TENDERNESS IN THE ANATOMICAL SNUFFBOX (between extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis/abductor pollicis longus) and pain with axial thumb compression. HIGH COMPLICATION RISK: AVASCULAR NECROSIS (AVN) of proximal pole and NONUNION (due to retrograde blood supply from radial artery entering distal pole). MANAGEMENT RULE: Initial radiographs are NEGATIVE in up to 20-30% of acute scaphoid fractures. If snuffbox tenderness is present, IMMOBILIZE IN A THUMB SPICA SPLINT AND REPEAT RADIOGRAPHS IN 10-14 DAYS (or obtain immediate non-contrast MRI / CT of the wrist).

subject: Surgery
topic: Open Fracture Initial Emergency Management Sequence
shortestValidSolution: Manage Open Fractures (Gustilo-Anderson classification): Bone cortex penetrates skin, exposing hematoma to environmental bacteria. CRITICAL EMERGENCY SEQUENCE: 1. IMMEDIATE INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS (administer within 1 hour: 1st-generation cephalosporin e.g. CEFAZOLIN for Type I/II; add AMINOGLYCOSIDE e.g. Gentamicin for Type III; add PENICILLIN if farm/soil contamination for Clostridium); 2. TETANUS PROPHYLAXIS (toxoid +/- TIG if unimmunized); 3. Remove gross debris, cover with sterile saline-soaked dressing, and splint; 4. URGENT OPERATIVE IRRIGATION AND DEBRIDEMENT in the OR within 12-24 hours. DO NOT irrigate extensively or probe in the ED.

subject: Surgery
topic: Posterior Hip Dislocation Presentation and Emergency Reduction
shortestValidSolution: Manage Traumatic Hip Dislocation: - POSTERIOR HIP DISLOCATION (90% of cases): Classic mechanism: High-energy MVA with knees hitting the dashboard with hip flexed. PHYSICAL EXAM: Affected limb is SHORTENED, ADDUCTED, AND INTERNALLY ROTATED (contrast with femoral neck fracture, which is shortened and EXTERNALLY rotated). topic: Necrotizing Fasciitis Diagnostic Urgency and Surgical Debridement
shortestValidSolution: Manage Necrotizing Fasciitis: Rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection of subcutaneous tissue and deep fascia. - CLINICAL HALLMARK: SEVERE PAIN DISPROPORTIONATE TO PHYSICAL FINDINGS, followed by woody induration, skin bullae (violaceous), crepitus (subcutaneous gas), and rapid systemic shock. - MICROBIOLOGY: Type I (polymicrobial: anaerobes + enterics, common in diabetics/post-op); Type II (monomicrobial: Group A Streptococcus [S. pyogenes] +/- S. aureus). - GOLD STANDARD MANAGEMENT: 1. IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY EXTENSIVE SURGICAL EXPLORATION AND DEBRIDEMENT (the single intervention that dictates survival); 2. EMPIRIC BROAD-SPECTRUM IV ANTIBIOTICS (Vancomycin + Piperacillin-Tazobactam + CLINDAMYCIN to block bacterial ribosomal protein synthesis and halt streptococcal toxin production). NEVER DELAY SURGERY FOR IMAGING.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Septic Arthritis vs Transient Synovitis Kocher Criteria
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Septic Hip from Transient Synovitis: KOCHER CRITERIA (each = 1 point): 1. Inability to bear weight on affected limb; 2. Fever > 38.5°C (101.3°F); 3. White blood cell count > 12,000/mm³; 4. ESR > 40 mm/hr (or CRP > 20 mg/L). INTERPRETATION: 0-1 criteria = low probability (transient synovitis; treat with NSAIDs and rest); >= 3-4 criteria = 93-99% probability of SEPTIC ARTHRITIS. MANAGEMENT FOR HIGH PROBABILITY: IMMEDIATE ULTRASOUND-GUIDED ARTHROCENTESIS (CSF/synovial fluid > 50,000 WBC with > 75-90% PMNs confirms) and EMERGENT SURGICAL ARTHROTOMY/WASH OUT to prevent femoral head osteonecrosis.

subject: Surgery
topic: Prosthetic Joint Infection Classification and Two-Stage Revision
shortestValidSolution: Manage Prosthetic Joint Infection (PJI): Classified by onset: - EARLY (< 3 months post-op): High virulence (Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negative bacilli). Acute joint pain, wound drainage, high fever. Managed with debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) if prosthesis is well-fixed. - DELAYED (3-12 months post-op): Low-virulence organisms forming BIOFILMS (COAGULASE-NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI, e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis; Cutibacterium acnes). Indolent course: chronic joint pain, persistent loosening, low-grade inflammation. MANAGEMENT: TWO-STAGE REVISION ARTHROPLASTY (Stage 1: Explantation of hardware + thorough debridement + insertion of high-dose antibiotic-impregnated cement spacer; Stage 2: Re-implantation of new prosthesis after 6-12 weeks of IV antibiotics and normalization of ESR/CRP).

subject: Medicine
topic: Fat Embolism Syndrome Pathophysiology and Clinical Triad
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES): Occurs 24-72 hours following traumatic long-bone fractures (FEMUR, TIBIA, PELVIS). Pathophysiology: Bone marrow fat globules enter torn venous sinusoids, embolize to pulmonary capillaries (lipase breaks down fat to toxic free fatty acids causing ARDS), and pass through patent foramen ovale or pulmonary circulation into systemic organs. CLASSIC CLINICAL TRIAD: 1. RESPIRATORY INSUFFICIENCY (dyspnea, hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrate on CXR); 2. NEUROLOGICAL COMPAIRMENT (confusion, delirium, stupor); 3. PETECHIAL RASH (pathognomonic: non-palpable petechiae in AXILLAE, CHEST, NECK, CONJUNCTIVAE). TREATMENT: SUPPORTIVE CARE (supplemental O2, mechanical ventilation for ARDS; early fracture immobilization prevents syndrome).

topic: Lung Cancer Screening Criteria (USPSTF)
shortestValidSolution: Manage Lung Cancer Screening Guidelines (USPSTF 2021 Update): - SCREENING MODALITY: ANNUAL LOW-DOSE COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY (LDCT) of the chest. - ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: 1. Age 50 to 80 years; 2. >= 20 PACK-YEAR smoking history (calculated as packs per day x years smoked); 3. Currently smoke OR have quit within the past 15 years. - DISCONTINUATION CRITERIA: Stop screening once the person reaches age 81, has not smoked for > 15 years, or develops a severe health condition that substantially limits life expectancy or ability to undergo curative lung surgery. Chest X-ray has ZERO role in screening.

subject: Medicine
topic: Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Screening Guidelines (USPSTF)
shortestValidSolution: Manage Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) Screening Guidelines (USPSTF): - ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: MEN AGED 65 TO 75 YEARS WHO HAVE EVER SMOKED (defined as >= 100 cigarettes in lifetime). - SCREENING TEST: ONE-TIME ABDOMINAL ULTRASONOGRAPHY. - THRESHOLDS FOR MANAGEMENT: - Normal (< 3 cm): No further screening; - Small AAA (3.0-3.9 cm): Ultrasound surveillance every 2-3 years; - Medium AAA (4.0-5.4 cm): Ultrasound surveillance every 6-12 months; - SURGICAL REPAIR INDICATIONS: Diameter >= 5.5 cm in men (or >= 5.0 cm in women), rapid expansion (> 0.5 cm in 6 months or > 1 cm in 1 year), or any symptomatic AAA.

strongestDistractor: No abdominal imaging is indicated because he quit smoking more than 15 years ago
distractorExclusion: While lung cancer screening stops 15 years after smoking cessation, AAA screening applies to any man aged 65 to 75 who has EVER smoked >= 100 cigarettes, regardless of when they quit.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Cervical Cancer Screening and Discontinuation Age Rules
shortestValidSolution: Manage Cervical Cancer Screening (USPSTF Guidelines): - AGE 21-29: Cervical cytology (Pap smear) alone EVERY 3 YEARS (HPV co-testing is NOT recommended under age 30 due to high transient HPV clearance). - AGE 30-65: Three acceptable options: 1. High-risk HPV (hrHPV) testing alone EVERY 5 YEARS; 2. hrHPV + Cytology co-testing EVERY 5 YEARS; 3. Cytology alone EVERY 3 YEARS. - DISCONTINUATION AT AGE 65: Discontinue screening if ADEQUATE PRIOR NEGATIVE SCREENING (3 consecutive negative cytology tests OR 2 consecutive negative co-tests within past 10 years, with most recent within 5 years) and NO history of high-grade precancer (CIN 2+) in past 20 years.

topic: Breast Cancer Screening Guidelines (USPSTF 2024 Update)

subject: Medicine
topic: Statin Therapy Indications for Primary Prevention of ASCVD
shortestValidSolution: Manage Statin Therapy for Primary ASCVD Prevention (ACC/AHA Guidelines): - 4 MAJOR STATIN BENEFIT GROUPS: 1. Clinical ASCVD (CAD, stroke, PAD) -> HIGH-INTENSITY STATIN (Atorvastatin 40-80 mg or Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg); 2. Severe Hypercholesterolemia (LDL >= 190 mg/dL) -> HIGH-INTENSITY STATIN; 3. DIABETES MELLITUS in adults AGED 40 TO 75 YEARS -> MODERATE-INTENSITY STATIN (e.g., Atorvastatin 10-20 mg or Rosuvastatin 5-10 mg); escalate to high-intensity if multiple risk factors or 10-yr risk >= 20%; 4. Adults aged 40-75 with 10-year ASCVD risk >= 7.5% -> MODERATE-INTENSITY STATIN.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Tetralogy of Fallot Hypercyanotic "Tet Spell" Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF: VSD, Overriding Aorta, Pulmonary Infundibular Stenosis, RV Hypertrophy): - HYPERCYANOTIC "TET SPELL": Triggered by crying, feeding, or exertion, which causes infundibular spasm or drops systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Right-to-left shunt across the VSD increases, sending deoxygenated blood to systemic organs -> profound cyanosis, tachypnea, syncope. - FIRST-LINE LIFESAVING INTERVENTION: KNEE-CHEST POSITION (or squatting in older children). MECHANISM: Flexing knees acutely kinks the femoral arteries, dramatically INCREASING SYSTEMIC VASCULAR RESISTANCE (SVR). Increased SVR reverses the shunt gradient across the VSD, forcing deoxygenated blood through the stenotic pulmonary outflow tract to the lungs for oxygenation. Secondary adjuncts: 100% O2, IV morphine, IV phenylephrine.

strongestDistractor: Decreases venous return to the right atrium, thereby reducing right ventricular end-diastolic volume
distractorExclusion: Decreasing right ventricular filling reduces pulmonary blood flow further, worsening hypoxemia; volume expansion is often beneficial in tet spells.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Coarctation of the Aorta Clinical Signs and Turner Syndrome Association
shortestValidSolution: Recognize Coarctation of the Aorta: Congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen, classically adjacent to the ductus arteriosus (juxtaductal). - ASSOCIATIONS: BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE (> 50-85% of cases) and TURNER SYNDROME (45,XO). - CLINICAL HALLMARK: UPPER EXTREMITY HYPERTENSION WITH LOWER EXTREMITY HYPOTENSION, accompanied by DIMINISHED OR DELAYED FEMORAL PULSES (RADIAL-FEMORAL PULSE LAG). - CHEST X-RAY: INFERIOR RIB NOTCHING (erosions on 3rd-8th ribs due to dilated collateral intercostal arteries) and "FIGURE-3 SIGN" on aorta. - CONFIRMATION: ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY or CT/MR angiography. Treatment: Balloon angioplasty / surgical resection.
necessaryInference: Recognize Coarctation of the Aorta: Congenital narrowing of the aortic lumen, classically adjacent to the ductus arteriosus (juxtaductal). - ASSOCIATIONS: BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE (> 50-85% of cases) and TURNER SYNDROME (45,XO). - CLINICAL HALLMARK: UPPER EXTREMITY HYPERTENSION WITH LOWER EXTREMITY HYPOTENSION, accompanied by DIMINISHED OR DELAYED FEMORAL PULSES (RADIAL-FEMORAL PULSE LAG). - CHEST X-RAY: INFERIOR RIB NOTCHING (erosions on 3rd-8th ribs due to dilated collateral intercostal arteries) and "FIGURE-3 SIGN" on aorta. - CONFIRMATION: ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY or CT/MR angiography. Treatment: Balloon angioplasty / surgical resection.
strongestDistractor: Takayasu arteritis involving the brachiocephalic trunk and subclavian arteries
distractorExclusion: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis that typically causes "pulseless disease" in the upper extremities with low arm pressures, unlike the upper extremity hypertension seen here.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Transposition of the Great Arteries Immediate Prostaglandin E1
shortestValidSolution: Manage Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA): Most common cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting in the NEONATAL PERIOD (first 24 hours of life). - ANATOMY: Faulty aorticopulmonary septum spiraling: Aorta arises from Right Ventricle, Pulmonary Artery arises from Left Ventricle -> TWO PARALLEL, INDEPENDENT CIRCULATIONS (incompatible with life unless mixing occurs via PDA, VSD, or PFO). - CLINICAL FEATURES: SEVERE CYANOSIS within hours of birth; HYPEROXIA TEST FAILS (PaO2 does NOT rise above 100-150 mm Hg on 100% O2). CXR: "EGG-ON-A-STRING" cardiac silhouette (narrow mediastinum due to AP vessel orientation). - IMMEDIATE LIFESAVING MEDICAL THERAPY: INTRAVENOUS PROSTAGLANDIN E1 (ALPROSTADIL) INFUSION to keep the DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS OPEN until emergent balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) or arterial switch surgery (Jatene procedure).

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Ventricular Septal Defect Natural History and Management
shortestValidSolution: Manage Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD, most common congenital heart defect): - SMALL RESTRICTIVE VSD (e.g., small muscular VSD): Loud, harsh, high-pitched HOLOSYSTOLIC MURMUR at LEFT LOWER STERNAL BORDER with palpable thrill; ASYMPTOMATIC, normal growth and development. NATURAL HISTORY: > 75-80% of small muscular VSDs CLOSE SPONTANEOUSLY by age 2 years. MANAGEMENT: REASSURANCE, regular pediatric outpatient surveillance, NO surgery or activity restriction required. - LARGE NON-RESTRICTIVE VSD: Softer murmur, signs of HEART FAILURE (failure to thrive, tachypnea, diaphoresis with feeds at 4-6 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance drops). Requires surgical closure to prevent EISENMENGER SYNDROME.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Kawasaki Disease Diagnostic Criteria and Treatment
shortestValidSolution: Manage Kawasaki Disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, medium-vessel vasculitis in young children < 5 years): - DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA: FEVER >= 5 DAYS PLUS AT LEAST 4 OF 5 "CRASH" FEATURES: 1. Conjunctivitis (bilateral, non-exudative, limbic sparing); 2. Rash (polymorphous, maculopapular); 3. Adenopathy (cervical, usually unilateral > 1.5 cm); 4. Strawberry tongue (erythema of lips/oral cavity with fissuring); 5. Hand/foot changes (erythema, indurative edema, periungual desquamation). - MOST FEARED COMPLICATION: CORONARY ARTERY ANEURYSMS (occurs in ~25% of untreated patients). - GOLD STANDARD TREATMENT: INTRAVENOUS IMMUNOGLOBULIN (IVIG, single high dose 2 g/kg) PLUS HIGH-DOSE ASPIRIN started within the first 10 days of fever onset to prevent coronary aneurysm formation.

topic: Subclinical Hypothyroidism Indications for Levothyroxine Therapy
shortestValidSolution: Manage Subclinical Hypothyroidism: - LAB CRITERIA: ELEVATED TSH (usually 5-10 mIU/L) with NORMAL FREE T4. - INDICATIONS FOR LEVOTHYROXINE THERAPY: 1. TSH >= 10 mIU/L (high rate of progression to overt hypothyroidism and cardiovascular risk); 2. POSITIVE ANTI-THYROID PEROXIDASE (ANTI-TPO) ANTIBODIES; 3. PREGNANCY OR PLANNING PREGNANCY / INFERTILITY; 4. Presence of symptomatic goiter. - If TSH is 5-9.9 mIU/L, patient is asymptomatic, non-pregnant, and anti-TPO is negative: REPEAT TSH AND FREE T4 IN 2-3 MONTHS (do not treat immediately, as ~50% normalize spontaneously).

subject: Medicine
topic: Primary Aldosteronism Diagnostic Algorithm
shortestValidSolution: Manage Primary Aldosteronism (Conn Syndrome): Autonomous excess aldosterone secretion from adrenal adenoma (60%) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (40%). - SUSPECT IN: RESISTANT HYPERTENSION (uncontrolled on >= 3 antihypertensives including a diuretic), HYPERTENSION WITH HYPOKALEMIA (often unprovoked or provoked by low-dose thiazide), or hypertension at young age (< 30). - DIAGNOSTIC SEQUENCE: 1. SCREENING: Morning PLASMA ALDOSTERONE CONCENTRATION TO PLASMA RENIN ACTIVITY RATIO (PAC/PRA ratio > 20 with PAC > 15 ng/dL); 2. CONFIRMATORY TEST: Saline infusion test or oral sodium loading (fails to suppress aldosterone); 3. ADRENAL CT SCAN to evaluate anatomy; 4. ADRENAL VENOUS SAMPLING (AVS) is MANDATORY to differentiate UNILATERAL ADENOMA (treated with LAPAROSCOPIC ADRENALECTOMY) from BILATERAL HYPERPLASIA (treated medically with SPIRONOLACTONE/EPLERENONE).

subject: Medicine
topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Diagnostic Testing and Splinting
shortestValidSolution: Manage Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Compression of the MEDIAN NERVE beneath the transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum). - RISK FACTORS: Repetitive wrist flexion/extension, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, hypothyroidism. - CLINICAL SIGNS: Paresthesias/pain in THUMB, INDEX, MIDDLE FINGER, and radial half of ring finger (sparing the thenar eminence because palmar cutaneous branch branches proximal to carpal tunnel). Symptoms worse at night. Positive Phalen test (flexion of wrists reproduces numbness) and Tinel sign. Thenar atrophy is a late finding. - FIRST-LINE INITIAL THERAPY: NOCTURNAL WRIST SPLINTING IN A NEUTRAL POSITION (relieves elevated intracarpal canal pressures during sleep). Second-line: Local corticosteroid injection; Refractory/severe: Surgical transverse carpal ligament release.

DYSPHAGIA (difficulty swallowing); 2. ODYNOPHAGIA (painful swallowing); 3. UNINTENDED WEIGHT LOSS; 4. Persistent vomiting; 5. Gastrointestinal bleeding / Iron deficiency anemia; 6. subject: Pediatrics
topic: Ileocolic Intussusception Non-Operative Reduction vs Emergency Laparotomy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Intussusception management: Most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children 6 to 36 months (idiopathic, hypertrophy of Peyer patches following viral infection). Clinical triad (present in < 50%): Episodic colicky severe abdominal pain (legs drawn to chest), vomiting, and "CURRANT JELLY" STOOLS (blood and mucus from bowel ischemia). Examination: Sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant, empty right lower quadrant (Dance sign). DIAGNOSTIC TEST OF CHOICE: ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND (demonstrates "TARGET SIGN" / "DONUT SIGN" on transverse view, and "pseudokidney sign" on longitudinal view). FIRST-LINE MANAGEMENT: If NO PERITONITIS AND NO PERFORATION: AIR OR WATER-SOLUBLE CONTRAST ENEMA under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance (both diagnostic and therapeutic; success rate > 80-90%). CONTRAINDICATIONS TO ENEMA: PERITONITIS, PNEUMOPERITONEUM (free air on X-ray indicating perforation), or hypovolemic shock. If peritonitis or perforation is present -> IMMEDIATE EMERGENCE EXPLORATORY LAPAROTOMY, NOT ENEMA!
necessaryInference: Identify ileocolic intussusception by clinical ultrasound target sign, and deduce that stable patients without peritonitis require non-operative pneumatic (air) enema reduction, while signs of perforation mandate emergency surgical exploration.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy with primary bowel resection and ileostomy creation

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Midgut Volvulus with Malrotation Diagnosis and Urgent Ladd Procedure
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Malrotation and Midgut Volvulus: Embryology: Failure of normal 270-degree counterclockwise rotation of midgut around superior mesenteric artery (SMA) during week 10. Result: Cecum is in right upper quadrant; duodenum does not cross midline; gut is suspended by a narrow mesenteric stalk; fibrous PERITONEAL BANDS OF LADD cross and compress duodenum. VOLVULUS: The narrow mesenteric pedicle twists around the SMA, causing acute duodenal obstruction and TOTAL MIDGUT ISCHEMIA/INFARCTION. Clinical presentation: SUDDEN-ONSET BILIOUS EMESIS IN A NEONATE OR INFANT (< 1 month of age). BILIOUS EMESIS IN A NEONATE IS A SURGICAL EMERGENCY! DIAGNOSTIC GOLD STANDARD: UPPER GASTROINTESTINAL (UGI) FLUOROSCOPY SERIES: Demonstrates duodenal C-loop failing to cross the vertebral midline, ligament of Treitz displaced to the right of the spine, and a "CORKSCREW" or "BIRD-BEAK" appearance of the twisted distal duodenum. Treatment: EMERGENT SURGERY (LADD PROCEDURE: untwisting volvulus counterclockwise, dividing Ladd bands, widening mesenteric base, placing small bowel on right and colon on left, and appendectomy).
necessaryInference: Synthesize that sudden bilious vomiting in an infant represents midgut volvulus until proven otherwise, diagnosed by upper GI series demonstrating abnormal ligament of Treitz positioning, and treated with emergent Ladd procedure to prevent total intestinal necrosis.
strongestDistractor: Immediate pneumatic contrast enema under fluoroscopy to achieve hydrostatic reduction of the volvulus
distractorExclusion: Contrast enemas treat intussusception; midgut volvulus is a twisting of the midgut around the SMA and requires emergent surgical untwisting (Ladd procedure), not an enema.

references.label: Millar AJ, Rode H, Cywes S. Malrotation and volvulus in infancy and childhood. Semin Pediatr Surg. 2003;12(4):229-236. PMID: 14655161.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia Immediate Resuscitation and Management
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH): Embryology: Failure of pleuroperitoneal membranes to fuse with septum transversum and esophageal mesentery during week 8-10. > 85% occur on the LEFT POSTEROLATERAL side (BOCHDALEK HERNIA; right-sided is Morgagni). Consequences: Herniation of abdominal viscera (stomach, bowel loops, spleen) into thoracic cavity causes SEVERE PULMONARY HYPOPLASIA AND PERSISTENT PULMONARY HYPERTENSION (PPHN). Clinical presentation: Neonate with severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, barrel chest, shifted heart sounds (to the right), and absent breath sounds on the left with bowel sounds in the hemithorax. IMMEDIATE DELIVERY ROOM RESUSCITATION RULES: 1. IMMEDIATE ENDOTRACHEAL INTUBATION! 2. BAG-VALVE-MASK (BVM) VENTILATION IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED! BVM forces air into the stomach and herniated bowel loops, causing massive gastrointestinal distension that further compresses the hypoplastic lungs and mediastinum, precipitating immediate fatal cardiovascular collapse. 3. Place a continuous-suction nasogastric or orogastric tube to decompress stomach. SURGICAL TIMING: CDH IS NO LONGER A SURGICAL EMERGENCY! Early surgery worsens survival. SURGERY IS DELAYED (often 48-72 hours) until pulmonary hypertension and hemodynamic stability are achieved (pre-ductal SpO2 > 85%, normal echocardiogram).
necessaryInference: Deduce that delivery room resuscitation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia strictly mandates immediate endotracheal intubation while avoiding bag-valve-mask ventilation, and that definitive surgical repair is delayed until pulmonary hypertension is stabilized.
strongestDistractor: Vigorous bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen followed by immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy within 2 hours of delivery
distractorExclusion: Bag-valve-mask ventilation is strictly contraindicated because it aerates the intrathoracic bowel and crushes the hypoplastic lungs; surgery must be delayed until pulmonary hypertension is medically stabilized.

references.label: Hedrick HL. Management of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia. Clin Perinatol. 2022;49(4):871-884. PMID: 36328608.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Necrotizing Enterocolitis Pneumatosis Intestinalis and Indications for Laparotomy
shortestValidSolution: Differentiate Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC): Most common gastrointestinal medical-surgical emergency in PREMATURE / VERY LOW BIRTH WEIGHT (< 1500 g) infants. Pathophysiology: Immature gut mucosal barrier + enteral formula feeding + bacterial colonization -> mucosal breakdown, bacterial invasion, transmural ischemic necrosis. RISK FACTORS: Prematurity, low birth weight, FORMULA FEEDING (breast milk is protective!), hypoxic-ischemic events, congenital heart disease. Clinical signs: Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance / gastric residuals, bilious vomiting, bloody stools (hematochezia), lethargy, temperature instability, apnea. DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK ON ABDOMINAL X-RAY: 1. PNEUMATOSIS INTESTINALIS (gas in bowel wall; linear or curvilinear radiolucencies parallel to bowel lumen; PATHOGNOMONIC!). 2. Portal venous gas (branching radiolucency over liver). MEDICAL MANAGEMENT: Bowel rest (NPO), nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole), TPN, serial abdominal X-rays every 6 hours. DEFINITIVE INDICATION FOR EMERGENCY SURGERY (LAPAROTOMY / PERITONEAL DRAIN): PNEUMOPERITONEUM (free intraperitoneal air on X-ray, seen as "Football sign" on supine X-ray or air under diaphragm on cross-table lateral/left lateral decubitus view), indicating BOWEL PERFORATION.
necessaryInference: Identify necrotizing enterocolitis by radiographic pneumatosis intestinalis in a premature formula-fed infant, and deduce that medical management is indicated initially, while pneumoperitoneum (free air) represents an absolute indication for emergency surgical laparotomy.
strongestDistractor: Immediate emergent exploratory laparotomy upon initial discovery of linear pneumatosis intestinalis
distractorExclusion: Pneumatosis intestinalis without perforation is managed medically with bowel rest, antibiotics, and serial imaging; emergency surgery is indicated only when pneumoperitoneum (free air) confirms bowel perforation or medical therapy fails.

references.label: Neu J, Walker WA. Necrotizing enterocolitis. N Engl J Med. 2011;364(3):255-264. PMID: 21247316.
